title: The Illegal Sacred Text That Can Never Be Destroyed
description: In the late 1990s, Saddam Hussein commissioned a 605-page Quran written entirely in 27 liters of his own blood. Today, religious authorities face an impossible legal deadlock. 📜🩸 How would you solve this theological paradox?
script:
There is a sacred text locked deep within a secure vault in Baghdad that presents a theological and legal paradox so severe it has paralyzed religious scholars and government authorities for over two decades. In the late 1990s, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein commissioned the creation of a 605-page Quran written entirely in his own blood. Today, the artifact sits hidden behind three locked doors, creating an impossible dilemma: Islamic law strictly forbids writing the sacred scripture with human blood, yet it equally forbids the destruction of any copy of the Quran once it has been created.

The origins of this surreal object trace back to 1997. Following the survival of his son Uday after a violent assassination attempt, Saddam claimed he had made a solemn vow to God to write the holy book using his own blood as an act of thanksgiving. Over the course of two years, a nurse routinely extracted blood from the dictator—ultimately totaling roughly 27 liters, or nearly seven gallons. To transform human blood into a usable medium for calligraphy, it had to be treated with precise chemical preservatives and anti-coagulants to prevent oxidation and allow it to flow smoothly through traditional reed pens. Master calligrapher Abbas Shakir Joodi was charged with the meticulous task of rendering all 114 surahs, spanning over 750,000 words.

When US-led forces entered Baghdad in 2003, the so-called Blood Quran was quietly removed from public display at the Umm al-Qura Mosque and locked away. Ever since, Iraqi leaders and Islamic clerics have been trapped in an agonizing theological deadlock. Under traditional Islamic jurisprudence, human blood is classified as ritually impure, or najis. Using an impure substance to write the literal word of God is considered a severe act of sacrilege and fundamentally illegal under religious law.

However, the paradox deepens because Islamic doctrine also strictly prohibits the intentional destruction, defacement, or shredding of any manuscript containing holy scripture. Burning or discarding the book would violate the revered text itself, regardless of the ink used to write it. As a result, neither Sunni nor Shia scholars can issue a definitive fatwa to burn the text, nor can they morally permit it to be put on display. The Blood Quran remains frozen in dark isolation—an untouchable monument to tyranny, trapped forever in an inescapable legal grey zone.
